How it reads the road

Check the road once, every close

The traffic light decides whether to drive, the throttle decides how fast, and speed limits and speed bumps decide when to slow down. Signals are calculated from 1x ETF closing prices, executed at next day's open.

View full research report→
01
Traffic Light
Still rising?
A green light means the close is above the 200-day moving average — go ahead; below it is a red light — pull over and switch to cash. A 3% yellow zone around the moving average prevents whipsaw stop-start.
02
Throttle
How chaotic is it right now?
Look at the volatility over the last 20 days — that's the road conditions. Smooth road, deeper throttle (up to 3x); bumpy road, ease off; above the threshold, pull over entirely into cash.
03
Speed Limits and Speed Bumps
Any reason to slow down?
When S&P sees CPI year-over-year rising, it's like a speed limit sign on the roadside: capped at 1x. Semiconductors don't switch gears again for 10 days after each shift — that's the speed bump; also, 30% of capital always sits in SOXX, running at a base speed regardless of road conditions.

Why not floor the throttle

Floor the throttle, or ride the road?

Holding 3x forever is flooring the throttle: in most years it does run fastest. But try switching the entry year to 2000 or 2007 — flooring it crashes into the wall and goes to zero,riding the road survives. That's the value of the rules: not winning every year, but not being knocked out in a crash year.

Run it ten years, where do you end up

Randomly reshuffled each year since 2000 into 4000 'future decades' to see where annualized returns land. Blue = as backtested; light blue = adjusted for your confidence in the backtest's excess return; gray = hold 1x forever.

Portfolio
50%
50% confidence · ten-year annualized median
—
Why discount it? How much confidence should you set?

Bootstrapping only handles 'the same rules with a different stretch of luck' — it doesn't handle 'this rule was picked out of 127 combinations.' The scale from the literature: published academic anomalies decay by about half on average (McLean & Pontiff 2016); under multiple testing, Sharpe ratios often need a 50%+ haircut (Harvey & Liu 2015). Our walk-forward and DSR both pass, so we can be a bit more optimistic than 50%; 100% would mean assuming the future exactly matches the backtest. The 1-year block bootstrap preserves the structure of multi-year crashes; structural breaks (like Japan after 1990) aren't in the distribution, so the real left tail is likely fatter. Not investment advice.

Conclusion

  • Most accurate danger signals: 20-day volatility, distance from 52-week high, trend.
  • VIX, credit spreadUsed alone, it sells at the bottom — only suitable as a cap.
  • Best: trend decides whether to be in the market + volatility decides leverage + MA50 fast re-entry (current aggressive tier).
  • Weakness is 2008; adding a credit spread cap can improve it, but costs about 3% less return per year — not adopted for now.

Conclusion

  • Only trend is reliable: after a sharp S&P drop, it rebounds quickly — volatility and VIX signals sell at the bottom.
  • The best is the simplest: MA200 ±3% 3x, about 1 turnover per year.
  • Weakness is sharp drops(2020, 2022); adding a volatility cap or fast re-entry doesn't help.
  • To reduce drawdown, lower to 2x, don't add more signals.

Conclusion

  • 20-day volatility is most accurate; trend has many false breakouts.
  • Best: MA200 ±3% 2x + volatility > 35% → switch to cash (already adopted by the site).

Conclusion

  • Macro signals alone cannot time the market: using macro signals alone for entry/exit, full-period drawdown stays below −78%.
  • The only single signal with real predictive power is "rate cutting":41% probability of a >10% drop within 3 months after the light turns on (vs 10% when not lit) — rate cuts are usually bad news; but the trend has already reacted, and stacking this on top doesn't improve drawdown.
  • "Rising CPI YoY → cap at 1x" is a genuinely useful cap:Drawdown -59.8% → -37.7%, all three segments beat 1x, annualized return is about 2.6 points lower; results are similar with 30–60 day delays and 6–26 week comparison windows, not a single lucky point. 2022 −49% → −18%.
  • Rate hikes, inversion, and CPI level as caps:Drawdown barely changes, only earns less.

Adversarial validation (2026-09-16, candidate pool of 51 macro variants)

TestCurrent MA200 ±3% 3x+ CPI rising (45-day delay, 63-day comparison) → cap at 1xSame, 126-day comparison

Applied to QQQ / SOXNo effect: QQQ annualized 19.0% → 15.5%, drawdown only from −62% → −54%; SOX drawdown unchanged. Only works for SPY.
  • It genuinely reduces drawdown:Confirmed by random signals and historical resampling, not just 2022's one-off luck; in resampled histories, the probability of exceeding −65% drops from 74% to 8–18%.
  • It doesn't add to returns:When ranked by annualized return, it's always near the bottom (47th / 51), PBO 83%. Its value is only in drawdown reduction.
  • 126-day (half-year) comparison window is more stable than 63-day:Bootstrap annualized return, probability of beating 1x, and drawdown are all better across the board; walk-forward has also selected it before.
  • Only works for SPY; not applicable to QQQ or SOX.

Conclusion

  • 50–100 days is too short:too many false signals, 3–17 turnovers/year, drawdown below −67%, consistent across all three markets.
  • 150–250 days is the same plateau:annualized return and drawdown are similar, no length particularly stands out; 300 days has the fewest turnovers but reacts too slowly.
  • A 3–5% buffer is necessary:the same MA without a buffer has 5–8x more turnovers and drawdown 10+ points deeper.
  • Most walk-forward cutoffs picked MA200, and in the block bootstrap, 150 / 200 / 250 have nearly identical annualized returns and drawdowns → 200 isn't a coincidence, but it's not sacred either; 150–250 all work.

Conclusion

  • A few genuinely show danger:NFCI > 0, Sahm rule, sector breadth < 50%, unemployment above 12-month MA — probability of a >10% drop within 3 months after lighting is 2–3x normal.
  • But stacking onto the current strategy is a net loss:by the time they light up, the trend layer has usually already exited; while still in the market, lighting usually happens early in a recovery, and being capped at 1x instead misses the fattest part of the move.
  • Breadth / relative-strength indicators are contrarian:after equal-weight or small-caps lag, subsequent returns are actually higher. Over these 15 years, big tech has dominated so strongly, and weak breadth is the norm, not a warning.
  • Seasonality, SKEW, US dollar, copper/gold ratio:no discriminating power, or lit half the days.
  • Use:not included in the rules, kept only as research background.

B. How to avoid being shaken out

⑥ Semiconductor volatility threshold wear: why is the broad market 3x but SOX in cash?

Phenomenon

  • SOX switches to cash because volatility > 35%, not a trend turning bearish. It correlates 0.84 with QQQ, but its volatility range is about double, so it triggers exit first.
  • Divergence is common: about 15% of trading days show 'broad market ≥ 2x, SOX cash'.
  • Recent volatility: 06/30 83% → 07/20 64% → 08/06 61% → 08/25 53% → 09/14 39% → 09/30 38%, hovering near the threshold.

Conclusion

  • Current single-day 35%: most turnover (about 20 times in the last 12 months).
  • Adding consecutive confirmation or hysteresis range: turnover halved; higher thresholds mean deeper drawdowns (−53% ~ −68%).
  • Divergence doesn't require cutting broad market exposure: 3 months after divergence, QQQ strategy median +11.1%, SPY strategy +13.6%.
  • Rule not changed for now; if changed, '35% for 10 consecutive days' has slightly shallower drawdown, half the turnover, about 0.5% less annualized return.

Extended conclusion

  • Relative threshold rejected: in long bear markets the percentile keeps rising with it, so the strategy never pulls out, and drawdown exceeds −73%; in walk-forward, no relative version holds up at −65%.
  • "High volatility and breaks below MA50" rejected: by the time of a crash the price has already fallen, meaning it reacts a step too late, making the drawdown even deeper.
  • "40% for 10 consecutive days": chosen in each of the first three walk-forward tests, ranked near the top afterward, and also caught up with 2025–26; but drawdown in resampled history is noticeably deeper.
  • Current 35%: smallest tail risk, at the cost of staying out of the market for long stretches during high-volatility bull runs.
  • Decision: keep the rule unchanged for now(2026-09-16). This is a trade-off between "fear of missing a big rally" and "fear of losing heavily in a crash" — no version wins across the board.

Close-to-close, rebalance to target weight whenever the multiple changes or every 21 days. Trading volume = annual buy/sell amount ÷ principal. The SPY aggressive track is fixed at 3x and SOX is fixed at 2x, so the share of 2x days depends on the strategy.

Conclusion

  • The gap is very small: long-term, the two approaches differ by only a few tenths of a percent — not a decisive factor.
  • Blended positions need monthly rebalancing to 50/50: without rebalancing, leverage can drift to 1.7–2.3x after a year; with rebalancing it slightly beats the 2x ETF (due to lower fees).
  • When the strategy switches between 1x, 2x, and 3x, blending is more cost-efficient: for example, going from 3x → 2x only requires selling half of the 3x holding, instead of converting the whole position into a 2x ETF.
  • Liquidity: QLD and SSO have far lower trading volume than TQQQ and UPRO, so spreads are usually wider; for large amounts, blending is easier to execute.
  • Semiconductors should always use the blended approach: USD tracks a different index, so it's inconsistent with SOXX signals.

Conclusion

  • QQQ, SPY: no change. None of a dozen-plus revisions passed. Averaging in the ensemble's deep drawdown from T3 and TV35 (15-year −62%) makes things worse; minimum holding, add-confirmation, and gradual scaling all cost 3–6 points of return without gaining win rate; VXN doubles turnover and costs 7 points of CAGR; margin-debt deleveraging comes closest (SPY 15-year drawdown −32% → −28%, 5-year win rate 92%), but it costs 1.3 points of CAGR with a 75-day quarterly data lag — not worth adding a layer for it.
  • SOX: all three candidates pass and can be stacked. Minimum holding 10 days (3-year win rate 64% → 69%, worst 3-year −33 → −22 points, bootstrap win-vs-1x 62% → 76%) + core 70% (15-year drawdown −44% → −37%) combined: 15-year CAGR 30.0% → 31.2%, drawdown −40%, 3-year win rate 70%, bootstrap win-vs-1x 82%, breach −65% 43% → 21%. The 5/10/20-day parameters all move in the same direction — not cherry-picked.Adopted on 2026-09-25: The site's SOX is now 'TV35 2x + no changes for 10 days after turnover + 30% SOXX always-on'.
  • ⑥'s '3 consecutive days to re-enter' is unchanged: Already covered by the 10-day minimum holding, no need to adopt separately.
  • Why only SOX can be fixed: SOX's whipsaws come from bouncing around the 35% threshold, so a 10-day cooldown directly addresses it; the 3-year periods where QQQ and SPY lose to 1x are slow bull-market consolidations like 2003–07 and 2010–12, where the trend layer enters late and exits early — any cooldown or confirmation would only make entries later.

Conclusion

  • In recent eras, SOX rotation almost never beats 1x: Post-2010 current version +25.4% vs holding SOXX throughout 24.9%, just with a slightly shallower drawdown (-42% vs -46%). The gap only widens to 4–10 points after 2015 and after 2020. The advantage is concentrated in 2000–09 (avoiding −85%)—exactly the era you think is a different time.
  • Cooldown days are noise: Two-way cooldowns of 5/10/15/20 days trade wins and losses across the four eras, with 1–3 point gaps and inconsistent direction; 10 days actually has the deepest drawdown after 2015. 'Only delaying additions' beyond 3 days clearly gets worse (missed rebounds).
  • Post-2010 bootstrap: no single cooldown length consistently wins: No cooldown beats 1x 62% of the time, 5 days 68%, 10 days 57%. All between 55–70%, not far from a coin flip.
  • Next-day execution hurts every cooldown length(−1 to −4 points), with no length particularly robust.
  • The honest conclusion: A 10-day cooldown isn't wrong, but it's not a well-founded optimum either; the real issue is that the SOX leg's edge is very thin in recent eras and is propped up by the 2000s. If you weight recent eras more heavily, the sensible move isn't to tune the days — it's to shrink the SOX leverage leg to a minimum, or even keep only SOXX 1x; QQQ already contains heavy semiconductor exposure.

B. Downside volatility: only count volatility on down days

The volatility layer currently uses 20-day total standard deviation, so even a sharp rally can reduce the position. Changed to only count semi-variance on down days (÷0.71 is the equivalent conversion under normality; ÷0.80 and ÷0.60 also listed). False-positive rate = the share of days where the volatility layer reduced the position but the past 20 days were actually rising.

Conclusion

  • 3-year win rate barely moves:All three approaches only move it by 1–2 points. The three-year segments where it loses to 1x are choppy whipsaw periods; no matter how you tune the leverage or cut costs, those segments still lose. Fixing that requires reducing whipsaw (signal ensembling, minimum holding period), not allocation.
  • Core/satellite improves how bad the worst case is:QQQ 70/30 worst 3-year excess return -16.0% → -10.5%, 15-year MaxDD -49.4% → -38.4%, bootstrap probability of drawdown breaking −65% goes from 72% → 48%; cost: 15-year CAGR +36.8% → +32.7%. This is a risk-preference choice, not right or wrong.
  • SOX comes for free:70% strategy + 30% SOXX, 15-year CAGR +29.1% → +30.0%, 15-year MaxDD -44.3% → -37.1%, bootstrap win rate vs 1x goes from 57% → 71%. Reason: the SOX strategy sits in cash half the time, and that 30% 1x position catches the gains missed during cash periods.Adopted on 2026-09-25(together with the minimum 10-day holding period from ⑭).
  • Downside volatility ✗:The false-alarm rate does drop from 60% to 40%, but performance worsens across the board (SOX 3-year win rate 64% → 46%). The high volatility that comes with a sharp rally is itself a danger signal (2000, early 2020, and late 2021 all saw a spike before the crash) — filtering it out removes half the alarm system.
  • Financing cost cap ✗:Sound in theory, but in practice 15-year CAGR is 1.4–3.3 points lower with roughly the same win rate. Short rates were above 4% about a quarter of the time, and in the last 15 years that period (2023–25) happened to be a strong bull market, so 3x still won big even after financing costs. Financing cost is already reflected in the synthetic returns and real ETF prices — no need to stack another rule on top.

D. Executing intraday — does it reduce losses?

Using the daily high/low/close as a proxy for intraday price, the signal triggers and executes at that same day's close, compared against the current 'signal at close, execute at next-day open' approach. Last 15 years.

IndexExecution method15-Year CAGR15-year MaxDDFull-period MaxDDTurnover/Year

Conclusion: CAGR gains 1–1.5 points, but drawdowns are mostly deeper (SOX 15-year MaxDD −44% → −60%), and intraday false signals don't show up in backtests. The hours saved by entering earlier get eaten back by false intraday breakouts.Keep close-based signals; intraday only gives one heads-up 30 minutes before close, without executing.

Conclusion

  • The longer you hold, the more stable it gets:QQQ win rate vs 1x 3-year 80% → 10-year 93%; QQQ +CPI win rate vs 1x 3-year 80% → 10-year 100%; SPY win rate vs 1x 3-year 80% → 10-year 100%; SPY +CPI win rate vs 1x 3-year 80% → 10-year 100%; SOX win rate vs 1x 3-year 69% → 10-year 73%; SOX +CPI win rate vs 1x 3-year 56% → 10-year 80%.
  • The worst 3-year stretches:QQQ entered 2002-10, lagging 1x by 18 points per year; QQQ +CPI entered 2002-10, lagging 1x by 21 points per year; SPY entered 2004-03, lagging 1x by 12 points per year; SPY +CPI entered 2004-03, lagging 1x by 12 points per year; SOX entered 2023-07, lagging 1x by 15 points per year; SOX +CPI entered 2023-07, lagging 1x by 26 points per year.
  • Entering at a top mostly beats 1x after 3 years:QQQ 2021-11 +103.5%(1x +28.4%), SPY 2007-10 +48.8%(1x -19.7%), SPY +CPI 2007-10 +48.8%(1x -19.7%).
  • The most damaging pattern is a rebound after a sharp drop(1 year later): QQQ 2025-02 -2.8%(1x +13.4%), SOX 2025-02 +47.5%(1x +59.6%).
  • Recommendation:Evaluate over 5+ years; large sums can be entered in stages over 6–12 months; first make sure you can stomach a −40% drawdown.

⑪ Holding all three markets together: can you average out the risk without sacrificing returns?

Three legs = the strategies used on this site: QQQ (fast re-entry 50% vol target 3x), SPY (MA200 ±3% buffer 3x + CPI-capped 1x), SOX (trend + volatility > 35% to cash 2x · 10-day no-trade after turnover · 30% always at 1x). Each rebalances by its own rules,On the first trading day of each month, rebalance the three portions back to target weights(including the portion sitting in cash).

Move only when ≥ 2 legs are in+19.8%+9.9%-46.1%32%
  • Do not move: Moving everything gives higher annualized returns in only 72% of paths, yet deeper drawdowns in 80% of paths.
  • A leg switching to cash is itself a risk signal: when the three markets are highly correlated, adding to the leg(s) still in the market means raising leverage precisely when risk is rising (at the extreme, it becomes 100% in a single leg).
  • The cash portion is the portfolio's brake: the equal-weight drawdown is shallow precisely because on nearly half the days at least one leg is in cash. Just park it in short-term bonds or a money market fund for interest.

Conclusion

  • The equal-weight portfolio's annualized return is not worse than any single strategy: full period +19.1%, drawdown -36.7%, worst year -26.9%(single strategy full period +18.9% / +17.0% / +17.1%, drawdown -64.9% / -33.3% / -53.3%). The annualized return isn't diluted, because weights are rebalanced monthly and the three legs go to cash at different times.
  • Drawdown falls in the middle: much shallower than holding QQQ or SOX alone; SPY with the CPI cap has the shallowest drawdown on its own, but also the lowest 15-year return. Resampling history, the equal-weight portfolio's probability of drawdown exceeding −50% is 20% (QQQ 95%, SOX 75%).
  • Do not optimize the weights: weights picked using past data end up nearly at the bottom afterward; equal weight or close to it is good enough.
  • Most other families don't apply: applying the same rules to Dow Jones, mid-cap, Russell, healthcare, energy, emerging markets, real estate, and long-term Treasuries all underperform 1x or hit −80% drawdowns. Leverage rotation requires assets with "strong long-term trend + volatility that gives early warning" — currently only technology / semiconductors / broad market qualify.
  • Add technology stocks as a fourth leg (25% each): full period +19.1% / drawdown -42.2% / 15 years +31.8%(three-leg equal weight +19.1% / -36.7% / +31.0%). It's highly correlated with the Nasdaq strategy, so diversification benefit is limited.
  • Today's three legs: QQQ 3x, SPY 1x, SOX 0.3x → the equal-weight portfolio's overall is about 1.4x.

E. Deflated Sharpe Ratio

After testing N combinations and picking the best, part of the best Sharpe is just the result of trying many. SR₀ = the expected best Sharpe out of N trials under pure luck; DSR = probability of "genuine skill" after removing that (Bailey & López de Prado 2014, with skewness and kurtosis corrections).

IndexAnnualized SharpeNumber of trials NLuck threshold SR₀Skewness / KurtosisPSR (without trial adjustment)DSR
QQQ0.591270.19-0.55 / 6.1100%98%

SOX0.601270.17-0.18 / 7.0100%99%

Conclusion

  • A. Cross-market: the rule isn't universal.The three rules only fully win on tech-heavy XLK (finance and biotech each win one rule); the other 10 indices (Dow, Russell, mid-cap, healthcare, gold, Treasuries, EAFE, emerging markets, energy, real estate) all lose to holding 1x. It's not fitted to a particular period — it captures the behavior of markets that are "high-growth, high-volatility, trend-persistent." Transplanting it to other indices will lose money — don't do it.
  • B. 1971–99: dodging bear markets is structural; without a bear market, it's a drag.S&P T3 3x, full period +15.7% vs 1x +11.5%, 1973–74 only captured -44.3%(3x holding -86.3%), 1987 single-day gap captured -33.2%(3x -69.5%). Nasdaq V2_50 3x +26.4% vs 1x +15.1%. But NDX rose steadily 1986–2000, and V2_50 +29.1% lost 1x +30.6%, with deeper drawdown: every exit was a false alarm. Drawdown of −53% barely broke the −50% threshold; the rule couldn't stop half the loss from a 1987-style gap.
  • C. Execution stress: QQQ and SPY are robust, SOX is not.With slippage ×3, fees ×2, one-day delay, and 10% missed turnover all combined, QQQ loses 3 points over 15 years, SPY loses 1 point; SOX alone, from just "one-day-late execution," +30.4% drops from +26.4%to, and 3-year win rate falls from 69% → 53%. Half of SOX's edge depends on timely execution — miss the order and it's gone.
  • D. Parameter cloud: QQQ and SPY are not cherry-picked; SOX has an element of selection.QQQ's adopted parameters sit at the 49th percentile within the cloud, SPY at the 32nd — 100% of parameters in the cloud beat 1x. SOX is at the 65th / drawdown at the 92nd percentile, with only 50% of the cloud beating 1x: switch to a different parameter set, and there's a 50% chance of losing to simply holding SOXX.
  • E. Deflated Sharpe: 98%–100%: after removing the luck threshold from 127 trials (SR₀ ≈ 0.19), the Sharpe ratios for all three markets remain significant. But this only answers "it's not pure luck" — not "the future will be the same."
  • Summary: QQQ and SPY's rules pass all four new-angle tests, only lagging during "decades without a bear market." SOX is fragile under both execution stress and parameter-cloud tests, so its position should be smallest; this aligns with ⑬ keeping 30% always invested and ⑭'s 10-day cooldown. Retirement planning figures should use B's full-period levels (S&P 15%, Nasdaq 26%, minus synthetic tracking error), not just the last 15 years.

⑰ Adversarial argument check: where could this whole logic be wrong

The previous section tested "whether the numbers were cheating." Here are the arguments that could invalidate the entire logicarguments,write clearly what can be tested and what can't.

Argument 1: "The unique characteristics of US big tech" is a rearview mirror — 1989 Japan had the same characteristics

Nikkei 225 1971–89 was a 20-year bull run, long trend, high drift; this framework would have passed back then. Then what? (CAGR / MaxDD)

Nikkei 2251971–19891990–20102011–2026
Hold 1x forever+18.1% / -36%-5.2% / -78%+13.6% / -31%
Hold 3x forever+32.0% / -84%-34.6% / -100%+22.5% / -75%
V2_50 3x (QQQ rules)+24.9% / -76%-7.8% / -88%+0.2% / -81%
T3 3x+20.4% / -83%-7.0% / -86%+6.5% / -78%
TV35 2x (SOX rules)+16.4% / -67%-3.6% / -71%+5.8% / -58%
T3 2x+16.9% / -67%-3.0% / -67%+7.5% / -58%

Holds.1971–89 the rules beat 1x (+24.9% vs +18.1%); after the bubble burst post-1990, the rules had 20 years of negative returns, drawdown −88% — the only difference from holding 3x is it didn't hit zero; after 2011 Japan stocks returned to a bull market, and the rules instead +0.2% vs 1x +13.6%— the market structure became "rally then chop," trend-following got whipsawed every time. The framework can pick out markets that "looked like" the past, but not whether they'll "still look like it" going forward. This is the system's biggest risk, and it can't be eliminated by backtesting.

Argument 2: the entire sample sits within the 1982–2021 long-term rate-cutting era — will it fail during a rate-hike / stagflation era?

S&P 1966–1982 (16 years sideways, two oil crises)CAGR / MaxDD

T3 3x+4.4% / -49%
T3+CPI 3x+4.4% / -49%
T3 2x+5.0% / -35%
V2_50 3x+6.3% / -51%

Partly holds.Over those 16 years the 3x rule ≈ holding 1x (4–6% vs 5.6%), similar drawdown; it didn't crash to zero (holding 3x −90%), but there was no edge either. Conclusion: in this kind of era it's "insurance that doesn't lose," not a money machine. Retirement planning can't assume the next decade will be like the 2010s.

Argument 3: the edge actually comes from just two periods — avoiding 2000–02, and the QE + AI bull market after 2010

Holds.Over the decade 2002–2012 excess return oscillated between −4 and +4 — essentially zero; the edge was concentrated in 2000–02 (avoiding the crash) and post-2010 (running at full throttle). The edge hasn't decayed as leveraged ETFs became more popular (it actually grew) — but that's because the market kept rising, which is exactly the shape of Argument 1.

Argument 5: the sample contains no overnight −20% like 1987 — what happens if 3x is running at full throttle when that hits?

IndexOriginal 15-year CAGRWorst-case insertion pointCAGR after insertionMaxDD after insertion1x same period

Doesn't hold (it survives).Inserting a −60% overnight gap for 3x on a day it's fully deployed, at the worst possible time, drops the 15-year CAGR by about 8 points but it still beats 1x; drawdown −63%. One 1987 won't destroy it — two would.

Arguments that can't be tested, but matter just as much

  • Crowding: TQQQ and SOXL are already tens of billions of dollars in size, and the rebalancing before close itself amplifies late-session volatility; MA200 is the most widely used signal — the more people exit on the same day, the bigger the opening slippage. The ×3 slippage test in ⑮C only covers part of it.
  • Product risk: issuers can liquidate, change fees, or do reverse splits; the 2018 XIV overnight wipeout is the same category of product. The backtest assumes the product exists forever and tracks the index at exactly ×3.
  • Regulation: the SEC has discussed restricting retail purchases of leveraged ETFs; sub-brokers may delist them. No matter how good the rules are, they're useless if you can't buy the product.
  • Yourself: the rules require you to buy back into 3x at the most fearful moments, like April 2020 or January 2023. The backtest carries no psychological cost; ⑬ shows the worst three years lag 1x by 15 points — whether you'd abandon the strategy during those three years is the real out-of-sample test.

Summary

  • The arguments that backtesting can disprove (window selection, single gap event) don't hold; the ones that can't be disproven (market structure change, stagflation, crowding, product risk, regulation, psychology) all point to the same thing:it's leverage on the structure of "US big tech's ongoing bull market," not an alpha independent of the market.
  • Japan is the only historical comparison we have, and the answer it gives is: the structure can change, and there's no signal before it does.
  • So position size matters more than the rules. This tool is suited as an execution tool for the thesis "I'm bullish on US tech" — position size should be decided by how much you can tolerate being wrong about that thesis, not by the backtested CAGR.
  • Howard's counterargument (2026-09-26): this is faith in America, and it's strong — constituent stocks keep renewing themselves, it's the world's largest market, technology keeps advancing, and a structural change isn't visible in the short term.Response: all three of these also held true for Japan in 1989 (constituent turnover, world's #2 market, tech leadership) — the difference was in valuation and capital structure. So the faith needs to be split into two layers:Structure(rises over the long run) → the reason to hold 1x, and the size can be large;Path(the way it rises — a long trend, slow declines, measurable volatility) → this is the actual reason to run 3x, and it depends on passive investing, the Fed's reaction function, and leveraged-product scale changing far faster than "American decline" would — 2022 was a preview. The system itself already separates the two layers: leverage only turns on when the signal is present = trust the structure, verify the path every day. The leveraged layer's size shouldn't be so large that it needs faith to hold up.

F. How could this fail in the future

⑱ Future scenarios and failure signals: how could this break in the AI era, and can we know in advance

Using a futures-studies approach: first list the five assumptions the system depends on to survive (A: long trend slow decline, B: volatility is measurable, C: the product exists, D: drift ≥ 10% with reasonable financing, E: checking once a day is enough), then ask which drivers could break them, expanding into six scenarios; finally map each scenario toquantifiable early signals, and test historically whether they have any lead time.

A. Six failure scenarios

#ScenarioAssumption brokenWhat happens to the systemWhat signal to watch
1AI bubble bursts (2000-style, but faster)
Data center capex proves unrecoverable, hyperscalers cut guidance in the same quarter, leaders gap down −25% in a day; 3–5 years of consolidation follow.		A: slow decline turns into fast decline, EAlive but a lost decade (shape of S&P 1966–82)CapEx outlook cut for two consecutive quarters, AI revenue / capex ratio fails to rise, NFCI turns positive; your "thesis stop-loss" clause
2AI super-cycle turns out real, but the path gets choppy
Tech keeps rising, but algos + 0DTE make ±5% intraday swings the norm; the trend holds, but it's a bumpy ride.		B: volatility becomes unpredictableNo loss, but badly underperforms holding 1x or even 3x (shape of Japan post-2011); the easiest scenario to make people abandon the rules at the wrong timeRolling 3-year win rate falls below 50%, volatility predictability < 0.5, 20-day volatility persistently > 30% but MA200 slope positive
3Structurally high rates + recurring inflation (1970s)
Deficit monetization, short rates stay 4–6% for the long run, CPI cap keeps triggering, stocks and bonds shake together.		D: financing cost, ASPY almost always at 1x (effectively useless); QQQ loses half its edge to financing costsShort rate > 4% for a full year, 10-year yield > 5%, CPI cap trigger ratio > 50%
4Regulatory and product risk
SEC restricts retail leveraged ETF access (actually debated in 2020), issuers liquidate 3x products after extreme volatility (precedent: 2020 oil / volatility ETFs), broker delistings.		C: productRules are right but can't be executed; forced liquidation mid-position = forced exit at the worst possible timeSEC proposals, TQQQ size / trading volume shrinking abnormally, tracking error widening, broker announcements. The only countermeasure is position sizing
5Geopolitical gap event (Taiwan Strait / key events)
Semiconductor supply chain re-rated overnight, SOX opens −30%, QQQ −15%, and not just once.		A, EThe SOX leg could go to zero in one shot, QQQ badly hurt; the only scenario that could wipe out the system in one strikeNo reliable signal exists; a rise in gap-event share is only visible after the fact. The only defense is minimum SOX weighting and three-leg equal weight as a pre-paid premium
6Market structure change (24-hour trading, AI agents exiting in sync)
Closing price no longer meaningfully reflects value; similar trend-following rules all exit at once, causing a stampede (2024-08 yen unwind was a preview).		E, BBacktest execution assumptions become unrealistic, costing 2–5 points per yearYour own slippage records (the system doesn't track this yet), gap-event share, volatility predictability

Scenario matrix: the system only makes money in the "trend continuation × predictable volatility" quadrant; over the past 15 years it spent 80% of the time in that quadrant, while 1966–82 and Japan 1990–2010 sat almost entirely on the opposite diagonal.

B. Do the signals have lead time? (historical test)

Each signal is sampled monthly; compare the median excess return of the three-leg equal-weight strategy over holding 1x in the 12 months after the light turns on, versus when it's off. If excess return is clearly worse and the loss rate is higher after the light turns on = the signal has lead time. Background color = currently lit.

Conclusion

  • Currently lit: volatility predictability, trend quality, short rate, SPY CPI cap trigger ratio. Short rate and CPI are signals for Scenario 3, and SPY is already capped at 1x, so the system is handling that on its own; low volatility predictability has been the norm the past two years (volatility clustering has weakened since 2022), and it's the one signal with real lead time — worth watching.
  • Has lead time: volatility predictability (median excess +5 points 12 months after light-on vs. +9 when off).
  • Inverted: rolling 3-year (+12 vs. +5), gap-event share (+12 vs. +6) — when these light up, a crash is usually already underway and the strategy is already in cash, so the following year tends to be its best. This means "the rules have lost recently" is not a signal to stop, but often exactly the time to stick with it.
  • Never lit: TQQQ tracking error, TQQQ trading volume — product risk hasn't occurred historically, so lead time can't be measured; that's exactly the nature of Scenarios 4, 5, 6: by the time you see it, it's already happened. The only defense is position sizing as pre-paid premium (minimum SOX weight, three-leg equal weight, leverage tier sized to survive an overnight −50%).
  • Action thresholds: Volatility predictability < 0.5 for a full year → treat the volatility layer as half-disabled, lower leverage cap one tier; short rate > 4% for over a year → accept SPY long-term 1x; product signal triggers → reduce position first then investigate cause; rule underperforms 1x for two to three consecutive years → history says wait, not leave.
  • What the system doesn't record: your own execution slippage. Scenario 6 depends on it alone. We recommend logging the open price and fill price at every switch, and comparing them every six months.

1. Adopted: QQQ fast re-entry volatility target 50% 3x, SPY MA200 ±3% buffer 3x + CPI cap 1x, SOX trend + volatility > 35% cash 2x · hold 10 days after switching · 30% always in 1x, TW hold 1x (no leverage).

2. Hedging means switching to cash; merely stepping down to 1x won't stop a crash.

3. Signals differ by market: QQQ watches volatility, SPY watches trend + CPI cap, SOX watches volatility and only uses 2x, holds 10 days after switching, and keeps 30% permanently in SOXX.

4. Returns depend on how much drawdown you can tolerate; using VIX or credit spread alone would sell at the bottom.

5. Adversarial validation: data is reliable, timing beats random; QQQ is most reliable, Taiwan stocks are unstable so no leverage is used. Actual drawdown could be 5–10 pts deeper.

6. Close to live trading: uses only real product multipliers, next-day open execution, and real ETF prices.

SPY · MA200 ±3% buffer, 3x + CPI cap 1x · Cash defense

Aggressive tier + CPI cap

Recommended strategy rules

Close above 200-day MA × 1.03 → hold 3x; below × 0.97 → cash. Additionally, when CPI year-over-year is higher than 6 months ago (45-day release lag), holdings are capped at 1x.

Signals are calculated using SPY close, executed at next day's open; exits always move to cash (short-term bonds / money market funds).

SOX · Trend + volatility > 35% cash 2x · No action for 10 days after turnover · 30% capital permanently at 1x · Cash defense

Semiconductor-dedicated tier + cooldown + core

Recommended strategy rules

Trend layer uses the same MA200 ±3% buffer; additionally, when 20-day annualized volatility > 35%, switch entirely to cash. Otherwise hold 2x. No further switching within 10 trading days after any switch (cooldown). These rules govern only 70% of capital; the other 30% always holds the 1x underlying, rebalanced monthly.

Signals are calculated using SOXX close, executed at next day's open; exits always move to cash (short-term bonds / money market funds).

Known limitations and next steps

Known limitations

  1. Synthetic data: leveraged returns for 2000 and 2008 are synthetic.
  2. Selection bias: picked the best from hundreds of combinations; real-world results are likely worse.
  3. Costs: excludes open-price slippage and taxes.
  4. Credit spread: uses BAA10Y as a proxy for HY OAS.

Next steps

  • Log actual signals and compare against the backtest after three months.
  • Backtest across a three-market combination.
  • Compare Taiwan-stock signal sources.
  • Whether to change SOX to a "10-day consecutive confirmation" rule.
